Vindictive

/vin-DIK-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Vindictive means having or showing a strong desire for revenge; vengeful.

Vindictive means having or showing a strong desire for revenge; vengeful. Losing the case made him vindictive: he spent the next year trying to get the opposing lawyer disbarred.

Worked Example

After the bakery review — two stars, 'promising but uneven' — the owner did not revise her recipes. She posted the critic's home address online, called his editor demanding he be fired, and left one-star ratings on every business his family owned. Even sympathetic regulars went quiet. A tough review deserved a tough response, they agreed, but this was something else: pure vindictive fury, aimed at punishing the man rather than fixing the bread.

The owner's campaign exists solely to punish the critic — address-posting, firing demands, retaliatory ratings — and that drive to take revenge is what vindictive means.

How Vindictive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

vengeful

vengeful: seeking to repay a wrong with harm

spiteful: acting from petty malice

Antonyms

forgiving

forgiving: letting go of wrongs

merciful

merciful: showing compassion instead of punishment

How Strong Is It? — resentful → vindictive → merciless

resentful vs. vindictive

resentful vs. vindictive: Resentful is weaker than vindictive: a resentful person nurses bitterness privately, while a vindictive one acts on it to punish.

merciless vs. vindictive

merciless vs. vindictive: Merciless is stronger than vindictive — merciless describes punishment without any restraint at all, while vindictive names the revenge-hungry motive behind it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vindic

Root — vindic: to lay claim to; to avenge (Latin vindicare)

Suffix — -tive

Suffix — -tive: tending to; having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Vindictive builds on Latin vindicta, 'revenge,' from vindicare — originally 'to lay legal claim to,' which drifted toward 'to claim satisfaction; to avenge.' Add the adjective-forming suffix and you get 'characterized by avenging.' The same root split in two directions in English: vindicate kept the courtroom sense (to clear someone's name — claiming justice), while vindictive kept the darker one (claiming vengeance). One root, two very different tempers.

Use the root in a new word: vendetta

Use the root in a new word: vendetta: A vendetta is a long-running feud of revenge — an Italian descendant of Latin vindicta, the same avenging root that fuels a vindictive grudge.
